title: Benchwork
subtitle: What the Armor Leaves Behind · Chapter 17 of 40
content:
Danse flirted like a man attempting to repair a radio with a combat knife.

That is to say: earnestly, dangerously, and without recognizing what he was doing.

We were at a weapon bench on the Prydwen when it started.

I had Righteous Authority disassembled for another adjustment. Danse stood beside me sorting components.

“You’ve improved,” he said.

“At weapon modification?”

“Yes.”

“Thank you.”

“You no longer install parts backward.”

I looked at him.

“There it is.”

“What?”

“You almost complimented me without insult.”

“That wasn’t an insult. It was an observation.”

“Your romance technique must be devastating.”

The component in his hand stopped moving.

I realized what I had said.

Danse looked at me.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“No. You said something about…”

“I was joking.”

His ears began to turn red.

“Right.”

I returned my attention to the rifle with the concentration of someone defusing a bomb.

Danse did the same.

For approximately thirty seconds.

Then he said, “For the record, I’m not attempting to romance you.”

I nearly dropped the barrel.

“I know.”

“Good.”

“Obviously.”

“Yes.”

Silence.

A scribe at the next bench quietly gathered her tools and left.

Coward.

Danse cleared his throat.

“I only meant that your technical skills have improved.”

“Understood.”

“And I enjoy working with you.”

My hands stopped.

He seemed not to notice the second sentence was far more dangerous than the first.

“I enjoy working with you too.”

“Good.”

Another silence.

He picked up the wrong screw.

I stared.

Danse looked down, realized it, and set it back.

“Don’t,” he said.

“I did not say a word.”

“You were going to.”

“I notice patterns.”

He gave me a look that should have melted armor.

Instead it made warmth spread through my chest.

That evening we took two beers to the observation deck.

Danse had called it “decompression after duty.”

I called it having a drink together.

He refused to call it anything.

The Commonwealth below was scattered with lights: Diamond City, settlements, campfires, places where people had decided darkness did not get everything.

Danse leaned on the rail.

“You ever think about leaving?” I asked.

“The Brotherhood?”

“The Commonwealth.”

He looked surprised.

“Where would I go?”

“Anywhere.”

“That’s not a destination.”

“Neither is purpose.”

He took a drink.

“You really dislike that word.”

“I dislike when people use it instead of wanting something.”

“Wanting isn’t always useful.”

“Neither is beer.”

“That’s debatable.”

I laughed.

Danse’s smile stayed after mine faded.

“What?” I asked.

“Nothing.”

“You were looking at me.”

“I do that sometimes.”

My own words, returned.

The air between us changed.

Neither of us looked away.

Danse’s face was different when he was not actively trying to be a paladin. Softer around the eyes. Younger. There was a small scar near one eyebrow I had never asked about. His mouth was more expressive than he seemed to realize.

I became extremely aware of it.

He looked at mine too.

Then a vertibird roared past the deck.

The moment broke.

Danse looked over the rail.

“I should check the duty roster.”

“At twenty-two hundred?”

“Yes.”

“Coward.”

His head snapped toward me.

“What did you say?”

“You heard me.”

“I am not a coward.”

“Then stay.”

I expected him to leave out of principle.

Instead he sat on the bench beside me.

“Fine.”

“Outstanding.”

“Don’t start.”

We stayed.

The conversation wandered into meaningless things, which somehow felt more intimate than confession.

Worst pre-War food we had eaten. Danse claimed canned imitation crab was a crime against humanity. I argued that the Brotherhood should revise its mission statement accordingly.

Favorite weapon modifications. Best places to sleep in the field. Whether a mirelurk counted as seafood.

“It lives in the water,” I said.

“So do things I would not eat.”

“That is cowardice again.”

“That word does not mean what you think it means.”

At some point our knees touched.

Neither of us moved.

The contact lasted long enough to become intentional.

Danse looked down.

Then at me.

“I meant what I said earlier.”

“About not romancing me?”

He shut his eyes briefly.

“No. About enjoying working with you.”

“Oh.”

His voice lowered.

“It’s… comfortable.”

For Danse, that might have been a declaration.

I swallowed.

“I feel the same.”

He nodded.

Our knees remained together.

No kiss.

No dramatic confession.

Just the Prydwen humming around us and a soldier who feared attachment allowing one small point of contact to remain.

Eventually Danse stood.

“Get some sleep.”

“There’s the romance technique.”

He groaned.

I grinned.

As he walked away he called back, “Good night.”

Not civilian.

Not soldier.

Just good night.

I sat there another minute smiling into my beer like an idiot.

His next attempt at flirting involved a torque wrench.

I was replacing the recoil compensator on a combat rifle when Danse appeared at the bench and set a tool beside my elbow.

“You’ll get better leverage with this.”

I looked at the wrench.

Then at him.

“Did you come all the way across the Prydwen to critique my leverage?”

“I was passing through.”

“You are carrying two cups of coffee.”

He looked down as if surprised to find them.

“One is for you.”

“Is it drinkable?”

“Yes.”

“That was not a confident answer.”

“I added sugar.”

“How much?”

Danse became suspiciously interested in the rifle.

I tasted it.

The coffee was still strong enough to strip paint, but someone had clearly attempted mercy.

“Danse.”

“Yes?”

“You remembered how I take it.”

His ears reddened.

“I remember operational preferences.”

“Sugar is tactical now?”

“It affects morale.”

I laughed so hard I had to set the cup down.

Danse crossed his arms.

“I fail to see what’s amusing.”

“You have been flirting with me for weeks and somehow you’re doing it through logistics.”

His entire face stopped.

I stopped laughing.

Oh.

There are moments when the Commonwealth seems to hold its breath just to see what stupid thing I will say next.

Danse stared at me.

“I have not—”

“You don’t have to—”

“I mean, I wasn’t—”

“Right.”

“Not intentionally.”

That shut us both up.

His eyes widened a fraction as he heard himself.

I leaned against the bench.

“Not intentionally?”

Danse looked as though he would have preferred another super mutant battle.

“I enjoy your company.”

The words emerged with the rigid precision of a formal report.

“I had gathered that.”

“I respect your judgment.”

“Sometimes.”

“Frequently.”

“Generous.”

“And I…”

He stopped.

His gaze dropped to the coffee cup.

“I notice when you’re not around.”

The room suddenly felt too small.

I let the teasing fall away.

“I notice too.”

Danse looked up.

We stood on opposite sides of a workbench covered in springs, screws, and a half-disassembled rifle.

It was not romantic by any reasonable standard.

It felt more intimate than a candlelit dinner could have.

He reached toward me, hesitated, then picked up the torque wrench instead.

“This fastener is going to strip.”

Before he could escape into the fastener, I noticed a small cloth-wrapped bundle near his elbow.

“What’s that?”

“Nothing.”

“Suspicious answer.”

“It’s a component.”

“For?”

Danse hesitated, then unfolded the cloth. Inside was a polished beam focuser, cleaner than anything available in the common parts bins.

I stared at it.

“You requisitioned this.”

“I located it.”

“With paperwork?”

“Yes.”

“For my rifle.”

“For Righteous Authority.”

“My rifle.”

He folded his arms. “You’ve been complaining about energy dispersion.”

“I complained once.”

“You were correct.”

I picked up the focuser. “Is this a gift?”

“No.”

“Danse.”

“It improves mission effectiveness.”

“Is that what Brotherhood officers call flowers?”

His entire face turned red.

“I have never given anyone flowers.”

“I believe you.”

He reached for the part. I pulled it out of range.

“Thank you.”

The embarrassment eased enough for him to meet my eyes.

“You’re welcome.”

There it was again. Care translated into equipment because equipment had specifications and affection did not.

I could work with that.

I installed the new focuser while Danse watched over my shoulder.

“Quarter turn,” he said.

“I know.”

“You’re over-tightening it.”

“I am not.”

He reached around me and put his hand over mine on the tool.

The correction became unnecessary almost immediately.

Neither of us moved.

His chest was warm against my back. His breath caught near my ear. For a man who could issue orders under gunfire without hesitation, Danse had no procedure for standing too close to someone he wanted.

“Quarter turn?” I asked quietly.

“Yes.”

“You stopped turning.”

“I noticed.”

His hand left mine with visible reluctance.

The rifle, at least, had the decency to remain uncomplicated.

I stared.

He stared back.

“That’s your retreat?”

“I don’t know what you mean.”

“Coward.”

His mouth opened.

Then he laughed.

Actually laughed, head dropping for a second as the sound escaped him.

It was warm and rough and so rare I forgot the comeback I had prepared.

When he recovered, he slid the wrench toward me.

“Use the correct tool.”

I took it.

Our fingers brushed.

Neither of us pretended not to notice.

The rifle took another twenty minutes.

The conversation took considerably longer.

prose_fingerprint: emotionally direct without flattening emotion into exposition
ground abstract feelings in concrete physical details, objects, weather, rooms, gestures, and sensory anchors
alternate compact emotional beats with fuller reflective paragraphs
let dialogue carry relationship pressure while narration carries interior consequence
use humor and ordinary practical actions to make vulnerable scenes feel lived-in rather than staged
favor character-specific reactions and small remembered details over generic declarations
allow grief, identity, survival, belonging, home, change, vulnerability, care, and autonomy to recur as thematic pressure
end scenes or chapters on an emotional consequence, changed understanding, concrete image, callback, or forward pull
preserve first-person immediacy and avoid omniscient knowledge outside Jasper's perception
use semicolons selectively for linked thoughts rather than mechanically
dialogue_fingerprint: continuous dialogue should sound conversational rather than like alternating speeches
interrupt dialogue with gestures, environment, hesitation, humor, and internal reaction
let characters dodge, misunderstand, tease, repair, and return to earlier wording
do not make every character equally eloquent, equally dominant, or equally emotionally transparent
relationship_fingerprint: slow burn must accumulate evidence: remembered preferences, repaired conflict, shared routines, private jokes, and practical care
attraction should not erase plot, outside obligations, individual goals, or conflict
vulnerability is strongest when it changes later behavior
after an intense/private interlude, resume with reconnection, humor, care, consequences, memory updates, and the next plot beat rather than treating intimacy as a reset
